_link.title: I can explain the relationship between surface area and rate of reaction using collision theory

toLevel2.stem: What effect does increasing the surface area of a solid reactant have on reaction rate?
toLevel2.answer: It increases the rate of reaction
distractors: It decreases the rate of reaction
It has no effect on the rate
It stops the reaction entirely

toLevel2.stem: Why does increasing surface area increase the rate of reaction?
toLevel2.answer: More particles are exposed for collisions
distractors: Each particle gains more kinetic energy
The activation energy is reduced
The particles change their orientation

toLevel2.stem: Which particles of a solid can participate in collisions with another reactant?
toLevel2.answer: Only particles on the exposed surface
distractors: All particles inside and on the surface
Only particles in the centre of the solid
Only particles that have been dissolved

toLevel2.stem: Powdered calcium carbonate reacts faster with hydrochloric acid than a large block because:
toLevel2.answer: more CaCO₃ particles are exposed to collide with H⁺ ions
distractors: each CaCO₃ particle has more kinetic energy as a powder
the activation energy is lower for powdered CaCO₃
the HCl changes concentration when powder is used

toLevel2.stem: Grinding a solid into smaller pieces increases its:
distractors: mass
kinetic energy
activation energy

toLevel2.stem: Increasing the surface area of a solid reactant increases the frequency of collisions with the other reactant.
distractors: False

toLevel2.stem: Particles inside a solid block that are not on the surface can still collide with the other reactant.
distractors: True

distractors: products

distractors: hidden

distractors: inside

toLevel3.stem: Why do many reactions involving solids depend heavily on surface area?
toLevel3.answer: Only the surface particles are accessible, so more surface means more possible collisions
distractors: Solids have lower kinetic energy than liquids or gases in all situations
Solids cannot react unless they are first converted into a liquid state
Surface area changes the activation energy of solid-liquid reactions

toLevel3.stem: How does grinding a solid into a powder dramatically increase the reaction rate?
toLevel3.answer: It greatly increases the total surface area, exposing many more particles
distractors: It increases the kinetic energy of each individual solid particle
It lowers the activation energy of the reaction with the solid
It changes the orientation of particles within the solid structure

toLevel3.stem: Why doesn't changing surface area affect the energy of collisions?
toLevel3.answer: Surface area determines how many particles are exposed, not their kinetic energy
distractors: Smaller pieces always have more kinetic energy than larger pieces
Surface area and kinetic energy are the same physical property
Energy of collisions is only determined by the mass of the solid

toLevel3.stem: Why is the concept of surface area mainly relevant for heterogeneous reactions?
toLevel3.answer: In heterogeneous reactions, reactants are in different phases and only the surface of the solid is accessible
distractors: Homogeneous reactions always have infinite surface area available
Surface area has the same importance in all types of reactions
Heterogeneous reactions never involve surface contact between reactants

toLevel3.stem: A cube of metal is cut in half. How does the total surface area change?
toLevel3.answer: It increases because the cut exposes two new internal surfaces
distractors: It stays the same because the total mass has not changed
It decreases because the pieces are smaller than the original
It doubles because the cube has been divided into two pieces

toLevel3.stem: Why is the total mass of solid used kept the same when investigating the effect of surface area on rate?
toLevel3.answer: To ensure that differences in rate are due to surface area, not the amount of reactant
distractors: Mass has no effect on rate so it does not matter if it changes
Changing mass would alter the activation energy of the reaction
Mass must change along with surface area for a fair comparison

toLevel3.stem: Surface area affects collision frequency because it determines how many solid particles are available to collide with the other reactant.
distractors: False

distractors: homogeneous

toLevel4.stem: A student reacts 5 g of marble chips with 50 mL of 1.0 mol L⁻¹ HCl, then repeats with 5 g of marble powder. Both are at 25°C. Which trial produces gas faster and why?
toLevel4.answer: The powder trial — greater surface area increases collision frequency with HCl
distractors: The chip trial — larger pieces have more total particles available
Both are identical — the mass and acid concentration are the same
The powder trial — the powder lowers the activation energy of the reaction

toLevel4.stem: A student investigates surface area by reacting zinc pieces of different sizes with sulfuric acid. Which variables must be controlled?
toLevel4.answer: Mass of zinc, concentration of acid, temperature, and volume of acid
distractors: Only the temperature needs to be controlled and nothing else
Only the mass of zinc must stay the same between trials
No variables need to be controlled in a surface area experiment

toLevel4.stem: A factory uses large chunks of limestone in a furnace but finds the reaction too slow. What change would increase the rate without altering temperature or concentration?
toLevel4.answer: Crush the limestone into smaller pieces to increase surface area
distractors: Use larger chunks of limestone to increase total mass available
Reduce the amount of limestone to decrease reaction time
Seal the furnace to prevent any gases from escaping

toLevel4.stem: Coal dust in mines can cause explosions while large lumps of coal burn slowly. Using collision theory, explain the difference.
toLevel4.answer: Dust has an enormous surface area, allowing rapid simultaneous collisions with oxygen
distractors: Dust has higher kinetic energy than coal lumps at the same temperature
Dust lowers the activation energy of the combustion reaction
Dust aligns more correctly with oxygen molecules for reaction

toLevel4.stem: A student measures the rate of reaction between magnesium ribbon and acid, then repeats with the same mass of magnesium powder. The powder reacts much faster. They explain this by saying 'the powder has more energy.' What correction is needed?
toLevel4.answer: The powder has more surface area, not more energy — energy per particle is unchanged
distractors: The explanation is correct — smaller pieces have more kinetic energy
The powder has less energy which is why it reacts faster
The powder has a lower activation energy than the ribbon

toLevel4.stem: Effervescent tablets dissolve faster when crushed before adding to water. Using collision theory, which explanation is correct?
toLevel4.answer: Crushing increases surface area so more tablet particles collide with water simultaneously
distractors: Crushing lowers the activation energy of the dissolving reaction
Crushing increases the temperature of the water around the tablet
Crushing increases the kinetic energy of the tablet particles

toLevel4.stem: Two identical experiments use the same mass and type of solid reactant. In Trial 1 the solid is in one large piece. In Trial 2 it is cut into 8 equal cubes. How does the total surface area compare?
toLevel4.answer: Trial 2 has a greater total surface area due to newly exposed internal faces
distractors: Both trials have identical surface area because the mass is the same
Trial 1 has a greater surface area because the piece is larger
Trial 2 has less surface area because each cube is smaller

toLevel4.stem: Coal dust causes explosions because its enormous {{blank:1}} area allows rapid simultaneous {{blank:2}} with oxygen.
distractors: cross-sectional
reactions

distractors: heating

distractors: colour

toLevel5.stem: A student doubles the surface area of a solid reactant and observes the rate approximately doubles. They conclude that surface area and rate are directly proportional. Under what condition might this conclusion not hold?
toLevel5.answer: At very high surface area, the reaction may become limited by the concentration of the other reactant
distractors: Surface area and rate are always directly proportional without exception
Doubling surface area always quadruples the rate of the reaction
The conclusion only fails if the temperature is also changed

toLevel5.stem: A peer claims: 'Increasing surface area is the most effective way to increase reaction rate for any reaction.' Evaluate this claim.
toLevel5.answer: Incorrect — surface area only applies to solid reactants; for solutions or gases, concentration or temperature are more relevant
distractors: Correct — surface area always has the largest effect on rate
Incorrect — surface area never has any effect on reaction rate
Correct — surface area is equally effective for solids, liquids, and gases

toLevel5.stem: In both the marble chips/acid experiment and the coal dust explosion example, surface area is the key factor. What is the common collision theory principle?
toLevel5.answer: Greater surface area exposes more solid particles for simultaneous collisions with the other reactant
distractors: Greater surface area lowers the activation energy of both reactions
Greater surface area increases the kinetic energy of the solid particles
Greater surface area improves the orientation of all collisions

toLevel5.stem: A student argues: 'If we could grind a solid to individual atoms, the reaction would be instantaneous.' Evaluate this reasoning.
toLevel5.answer: Not necessarily — the rate would also depend on collision energy, orientation, and concentration of the other reactant
distractors: Correct — individual atoms would react instantly with any other reactant
Incorrect — grinding to atoms would prevent any reaction from occurring
Correct — surface area is the only factor that limits any reaction rate

toLevel5.stem: Compare the effect of surface area on rate with the effect of concentration on rate. What do they have in common?
toLevel5.answer: Both increase collision frequency without changing the energy or orientation of collisions
distractors: Both increase the kinetic energy of colliding particles equally
Both lower the activation energy of the reaction by the same amount
Both change the orientation of particles during every collision

toLevel5.stem: A student states: 'Surface area has no effect on the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution.' Is this correct and why?
toLevel5.answer: Correct — surface area does not change temperature or particle energies, so the distribution is unaffected
distractors: Incorrect — increasing surface area shifts the curve to the right
Incorrect — increasing surface area makes the curve taller and narrower
Correct — but only because Maxwell-Boltzmann curves cannot be drawn for solids

toLevel5.stem: In a reaction where excess acid is used, both a powder and a large piece of the same solid will eventually produce the same total amount of product. Why?
toLevel5.answer: The same mass of solid is the limiting reagent in both cases — surface area only affects the rate, not the yield
distractors: The powder produces more total product because it reacts faster
The large piece produces more product because it has more total particles
Surface area determines both the rate and the total amount of product formed

toLevel5.stem: A student proposes using a solid catalyst as a fine powder rather than large pellets. Using collision theory, evaluate whether this would improve its effectiveness.
toLevel5.answer: Yes — more catalyst surface area means more reactant particles can access the catalytic surface
distractors: No — the form of the catalyst has no effect on how well it works
No — only the chemical identity of the catalyst matters, not its surface area
Yes — but only because powdered catalysts lower Ea more than pellets do
